The famous squid hunter, the giant seal, or the third one? Scientists glued satellite tags to all of them and one went down almost three kilometres and, on another dive, stayed under for longer than a feature film. Its lungs collapse on purpose.
Which did you pick?

research.topic: Deepest and longest dives recorded for any mammal: Cuvier's beaked whale (Ziphius cavirostris). Schorr et al. (PLoS ONE, 2014) tagged eight whales off Southern California and logged a dive to 2,992 m (and one of 137.5 min). Quick et al. (Journal of Experimental Biology, 2020) analysed 3,680 dives from 23 whales off Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and recorded a dive of 222 min (3 h 42 min), the longest for any mammal. Sperm whales are recorded to about 2,250 m; southern elephant seals to about 2,388 m. Beaked whales survive by letting the lungs collapse, slowing the heart and storing oxygen in muscle myoglobin; at 3,000 m the pressure is roughly 300 atmospheres.

myths.myth: The sperm whale, the famous squid hunter, is the deepest-diving mammal.
myths.reality: Sperm whales reach about 2,250 m; the deepest dive ever recorded for a mammal is a Cuvier's beaked whale at 2,992 m, and the same species holds the duration record at 222 minutes.

landscape.our_gap: Deep-dive clips are top-10 lists with stock footage; nobody drops the three depths to scale, raises the record-holder out of the basin where it was tagged and pins the second record site as a quiz.
